fields.subtitle: Is It True? Who Am I? Honest questions and the God who answers them
fields.description: Thirty daily devotions for readers aged 13 to 17 that take the big questions seriously: Is God real? Can I trust the Bible? Did Jesus really rise? Who am I when my feed says otherwise? And what does it cost to follow Him for real? Each day has a Bible passage, a short honest teaching, a question, something to try, a prayer, and a pointer to a classic in the library that goes deeper. The first book of Anchored.
fields.about_html:
Anchored is an original Ochorus devotional series for readers aged 13 to 17, the next step for those who have grown out of Rooted. Its picture comes from Hebrews 6:19: “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure.” An anchor does not stop the storm. It holds the boat while the storm passes, and the teenage years bring plenty of weather.

Book 1 has three parts of ten days. Is It True? gives real reasons for faith: doubt and Thomas, the case for God, the Bible, the history of Jesus and His resurrection, suffering, science and the claim that Jesus is the only way. Who Am I? turns to identity: made in God’s image, known completely, the gap between the real you and your feed, comparison, failure, anxiety, loneliness and belonging. Following for Real counts the cost: standing alone, temptation, purity, what you post, friends, parents, prayer and hearing God.

Every day ends with Go deeper: one chapter from a classic in the Ochorus library where Christians who asked the same questions long ago found their answers, from Augustine and Pascal to Chesterton and Lewis. Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible.

qa.question: What is Anchored – 30 Days with God for Teens?
qa.answer: A series of daily devotions for readers aged 13 to 17. Each day has a Bible passage, a short teaching that takes hard questions seriously, a question to think about, something to try, a prayer, and a pointer to one chapter of a Christian classic that goes deeper. This is Book 1.

qa.question: What does Book 1 cover?
qa.answer: Three parts of ten days. Is It True? looks at the reasons for faith, from the existence of God to the resurrection. Who Am I? is about identity, comparison, failure, anxiety and belonging. Following for Real is about the cost of following Jesus: standing alone, temptation, purity, friends, parents and prayer.

qa.question: Is it all right to have doubts?
qa.answer: Yes. Book 1 begins with Thomas, who doubted the resurrection until he saw Jesus, and Jesus met him with evidence rather than a rebuke. The book treats honest questions with respect and gives real reasons, not slogans.

qa.question: What is the Go deeper section?
qa.answer: Each day ends by pointing to one chapter of a classic in the Ochorus library, such as Pascal’s Pensées, Chesterton’s Orthodoxy or Augustine’s Confessions, where believers who asked the same question long ago worked out an answer. All of them are free to read.

qa.question: Who is it for?
qa.answer: Readers aged 13 to 17, to read on their own or with a youth group or parent. Younger readers can start with Rooted, the series for ages 9 to 12.

qa.question: Which Bible translation does it use?
qa.answer: Every Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible (BSB), a modern and readable translation that is in the public domain.

fields.title: Introduction: Welcome to Anchored
fields.body_html:
Stand on any shore where boats are kept, whether it’s a harbour, a fishing beach on a lake or a muddy river bank, and watch what happens when the weather turns. The wind picks up. The water gets rough. Boats that aren’t tied to anything start to drift, and some of them end up on the rocks. But the boats that are anchored swing round to face the wind and stay exactly where they are.

An anchor doesn’t stop the storm. The waves still come and the boat still rocks. What an anchor does is hold. It reaches down past the surface, where everything is moving, and grips something that isn’t moving at all.

That picture comes straight from the Bible:

“We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf.”

— Hebrews 6:19–20 (BSB)

The writer is saying that a Christian’s hope isn’t fastened to a mood, a good week or a feeling at a youth camp. It’s fastened to Jesus Himself, who has gone ahead of us into the very presence of God. He is the fixed point. When everything on the surface of your life is moving, He isn’t.

And at your age, a lot is moving: your body, your friendships, your family, your exams, the phone that never stops buzzing. You may also be asking questions you didn’t ask when you were ten. Is any of this actually true? Who am I, really? Does following Jesus work in real life? Those are good questions. This book is written for people who are asking them.

What’s in this book

This is Book 1 of Anchored, and its thirty days come in three parts:

  • Part 1 · Is It True? (Days 1–10). Doubt, God, the Bible, the historical Jesus, the resurrection, suffering, science, other religions and the times when God feels silent.
  • Part 2 · Who Am I? (Days 11–20). What God says about you: made in His image, completely known, more than your feed, free from the comparison trap, forgiven when you’ve blown it, not alone when you’re anxious or lonely, and adopted into His family.
  • Part 3 · Following for Real (Days 21–30). What following Jesus looks like with your actual life: counting the cost, standing alone, temptation, purity, what you post, who your friends are, your parents, prayer, hearing God, and holding on.

Along the way, Day 8 includes a clear invitation to trust Jesus for yourself. If you’ve never done that, take your time with that day.

How each day works

Each day takes about ten minutes and has six parts:

  1. The verse. A passage from the Bible. Read it slowly.
  2. The teaching. A few minutes of reading that unpacks the passage and what it has to do with your life.
  3. Think about it. One or two honest questions. Think them through, write down your answer or talk about it with someone you trust.
  4. Try this. One concrete thing to do today.
  5. Go deeper. A classic from the Ochorus library, written by Christians who asked the same questions long ago. Pascal, Chesterton, Bunyan, Augustine and the others weren’t people who never doubted. Many of them wrestled with exactly what you’re wrestling with, and what they found is still worth reading. Each day names the chapter to start with.
  6. The prayer. A short prayer you can pray as it is, or use as a starting point for your own words.

A few tips

  • Pick a time and a place. Before school, on the bus, after dinner, before you sleep. The same time each day turns it into a habit.
  • Use a Bible. Look up the passage in a printed Bible or a Bible app and read the verses around it.
  • Write things down. Keep a notebook or a notes file for your answers, your questions and your prayers. A question you write down today might be answered on a day you don’t expect.
  • Don’t do it alone. Read alongside a friend, a brother or sister, a parent or a youth leader, and compare notes.
  • Bring your questions. If something here doesn’t convince you, don’t pretend it does. Ask God about it, and ask a Christian you trust. Faith that has faced its questions is stronger than faith that never looked.
  • Missed a day? That’s fine. This isn’t a streak to protect. Just pick up where you left off. God isn’t keeping score, and He’s glad you’re here.

One honest word before you start: this book can’t make you a Christian, and reading it won’t make you grow. Only God does that. But He has promised that people who seek Him with their whole heart will find Him. Thirty days of seeking is a good place to begin.

Let’s drop anchor.

For parents, grandparents and leaders

Anchored is written for readers aged 13 to 17 to read on their own, though it works just as well alongside an adult or in a small group, and the “Think about it” questions make good conversation starters. It takes teenagers’ questions seriously and gives real reasons rather than slogans. Each day’s Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible. Day 8 includes a clear, gentle invitation to trust Christ; if your teen responds, please talk it through with them. Two days speak plainly about sensitive subjects: Day 16 on anxiety and Day 24 on purity. Both are written with care, and both point the reader to a parent or trusted adult. You may want to read those days first.

fields.title: Day 1 — Doubt Is Allowed
fields.body_html:
“‘If You can?’ echoed Jesus. ‘All things are possible to him who believes!’ Immediately the boy’s father cried out, ‘I do believe; help my unbelief!’”

— Mark 9:23–24 (BSB)

It’s late. Everyone else at home is asleep, and you’re lying awake with a thought you’d never say out loud at church: What if none of it is true? Maybe it came from a video someone dropped in the group chat. Maybe a teacher said religion is something people invent to feel better. Maybe it just arrived on its own. And right behind it comes a heavier thought: If I’m doubting, maybe I’m not a real Christian at all.

Start here: doubt is not the opposite of faith. The Bible is full of people with questions, and God didn’t throw any of them out. Even on the mountain where the disciples met the risen Jesus, Matthew says plainly, “they worshiped Him, but some doubted.”

Look at the man in Mark 9. His son had been suffering for years. The disciples had tried to help and failed. By the time he reached Jesus, his hope was worn thin: “If You can do anything, have compassion on us and help us.” Jesus picked up on that if. And the father answered with one of the most honest sentences in the whole Bible: “I do believe; help my unbelief!”

He was holding belief and unbelief in the same hand, and he didn’t pretend otherwise. Jesus didn’t tell him to come back when he’d sorted himself out. He healed the boy that same day.

Or think of Thomas. After the resurrection, the other disciples told him, “We have seen the Lord!” Thomas wasn’t having it: “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands, and put my finger where the nails have been, and put my hand into His side, I will never believe.” A week later Jesus came back, and He went straight to Thomas. No lecture. He offered Thomas exactly the evidence he’d asked for. And the doubter made the boldest statement of faith in the whole Gospel: “My Lord and my God!”

So there are two kinds of doubt. One kind folds its arms and says, “Nothing could convince me, and I’m not going to look.” The other says, “I want to know what’s true, so I’m going to ask.” The first kind closes a door. The second kind knocks on it. And Jesus said, “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and the door will be opened to you.”

Christianity can handle your questions. It’s built on things that happened in real places to real people, which means it can be examined. Over the next nine days we’ll look at some of the biggest questions there are: whether God exists, whether the Bible can be trusted, whether Jesus really lived and really rose, and why there’s so much suffering. You won’t get slogans. You’ll get reasons.

But notice where the father in Mark 9 took his doubt. He didn’t take it away from Jesus. He took it to Jesus. That’s the move. Your questions don’t have to be a wall between you and God. They can be the very thing you bring to Him.

Think about it: What’s one question about God or the Bible that you’ve wondered about but never said out loud? Who could you safely ask about it?

Try this: Write your biggest question at the top of a fresh page in a notebook or notes app. Over the next ten days, add anything that helps you answer it.

Go deeper: Orthodoxy by G. K. Chesterton — Chesterton explains that he set out to invent a daring new philosophy of his own, and discovered, with some embarrassment and a lot of joy, that what he had found was the old Christian faith. Start with chapter 2, “Introduction in Defence of Everything Else”.

Lord Jesus, I do believe; help my unbelief. You know the questions I carry, even the ones I’m afraid to say out loud. Thank You that You didn’t turn away Thomas or the father in Mark 9, and that You won’t turn me away either. Lead me into what is true, and give me the courage to keep knocking. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 2 — Is There a God?
fields.body_html:
“For what may be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it plain to them. For since the creation of the world God’s invisible qualities, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship, so that men are without excuse.”

— Romans 1:19–20 (BSB)

Some questions are bigger than others. “Is there a God?” might be the biggest of all, because the answer changes the meaning of everything else.

Paul says that God’s “eternal power and divine nature” have been “clearly seen, being understood from His workmanship.” In other words, the world itself is a signpost. You don’t need a laboratory or a philosophy degree to read it. A girl herding goats in the Ethiopian highlands and a student in a lecture hall in Seoul are looking at the same evidence.

So where does that evidence point? Think about three signposts.

First, there is something rather than nothing. Everything you’ve ever seen that began to exist had a cause: your phone, your house, you. Most scientists today agree that the universe itself had a beginning. So what caused that? Whatever it was had to be outside time, space and matter, and powerful enough to bring them all into being. That sounds a great deal like what the Bible calls God.

Second, the universe makes sense. It runs on laws so steady that we can write them down as mathematics, launch a spacecraft at a planet that is moving through space, and arrive years later exactly on target. Why should the universe be orderly at all? And why should our minds be able to understand it? If everything came from mindless chance, that’s a very strange coincidence. If it came from a Mind, it’s exactly what you’d expect.

Third, there’s something inside you. You know that some things are truly wrong, not just unpopular: bullying someone weaker, betraying a friend, cruelty for fun. Where does that sense of ought come from? And you carry a longing that nothing in this world quite fills. The thing you wanted so badly turns out, once you have it, to be not quite enough. That ache makes sense if you were made for Someone.

None of these signposts forces you to believe. They aren’t like a maths proof that leaves you no choice. Blaise Pascal, the brilliant French mathematician who built one of the first calculating machines, put it like this: there is enough light for those who want to see, and enough darkness for those who don’t. God isn’t trying to win an argument. He wants to be known and loved, and love can’t be forced.

And here is the most surprising part. The God behind the universe isn’t a distant force. When Paul spoke to the philosophers of Athens, he told them that God made people so “that they would seek Him and perhaps reach out for Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.”

Not far. Not from them, and not from you.

Think about it: Which of the three signposts seems strongest to you? Which seems weakest, and why?

Try this: Spend five minutes outside today, or at a window, with your phone in another room. Look closely at one living thing. Ask yourself honestly where you think it came from.

Go deeper: Pensées by Blaise Pascal — in his famous “wager”, Pascal argues that nobody can stay neutral about God, and that there are only two kinds of reasonable people: those who serve God with all their heart because they know Him, and those who seek Him with all their heart because they don’t know Him yet. Start with chapter 3, “Of the Necessity of the Wager”.

Creator God, thank You for a world full of signposts pointing back to You. Open my eyes to see what You have made plain. When I’m not sure, help me keep seeking instead of giving up. Thank You that You are not far from me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 3 — Can I Trust the Bible?
fields.body_html:
“All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.”

— 2 Timothy 3:16–17 (BSB)

Someone in your class says it with total confidence: “The Bible’s been changed so many times that nobody knows what it originally said.” It sounds convincing. Is it true?

Start with what the Bible claims about itself. Paul tells Timothy, “All Scripture is God-breathed.” Real people wrote it: shepherds, kings, fishermen, a doctor, a tax collector. You can hear their different personalities on the page. But behind their words is God’s own breath. He spoke through them, so what they wrote is what He meant to say.

Of course, a book claiming to come from God doesn’t prove that it does. So here are some reasons to take that claim seriously.

It holds together. About forty writers, over roughly fifteen hundred years, in three languages, wrote the books of the Bible. Many of them never met. Yet it tells one story from beginning to end: God creating, people turning away from Him, and God coming to the rescue through Jesus.

It was copied with remarkable care. We don’t have the original pages written by Paul or Luke, but then we don’t have the originals of any ancient book. What we have are copies. For most ancient writers that means a handful of copies, often made many centuries later. For the New Testament, scholars have more than five thousand handwritten copies in Greek alone, some of them made within a few generations of the originals. With that many copies from so many places, scholars can compare them and spot where a tired scribe slipped. Most of the differences are spelling and small copying mistakes, and none of them overturns a central belief of the Christian faith.

It has been tested. In the 1940s, the story goes, a young shepherd near the Dead Sea threw a stone into a cave and heard pottery break. The jars inside held ancient scrolls, among them a complete copy of Isaiah about a thousand years older than any Hebrew copy known before. When scholars compared the two, the wording was overwhelmingly the same.

But the best test is the one Paul gives in the very same sentence. Scripture is “useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” In other words, it does something. It doesn’t just sit there being old. It reads you while you read it. It shows you your own heart, puts you right, and trains you to live differently.

Derek Prince was a brilliant young philosopher at Cambridge who thought the Bible was one ancient book among many. When the Second World War came, he took a Bible into the army and began reading it straight through, as an intellectual exercise. Months later, in a barrack room, he wasn’t analysing it any more. He had met the Person it talks about.

You don’t have to settle every question before you open the Bible. Read it honestly, and see what happens.

Think about it: What have you heard people say against the Bible? Which of today’s reasons speaks to it most directly?

Try this: Pick one short book of the Bible, such as Mark, Philippians or James, and start reading it straight through this week, a chapter a day, asking only: What does it actually say?

Go deeper: The Key Teachings of Derek Prince — tells how a sceptical Cambridge philosopher read the Bible through for some nine months as a soldier and came out convinced of two things he said for sixty years: that Jesus Christ is alive, and that the Bible is true. Start with chapter 2, “The Philosopher in the Barrack Room”.

Is it true? Start with what the Bible claims about itself. Paul tells Timothy, “All Scripture is God-breathed.” Real people wrote it: shepherds, kings, fishermen, a doctor, a tax collector. fields.title: Day 4 — Was Jesus Real?
fields.body_html:
“Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.”

— Luke 1:1–4 (BSB)

Every so often a post goes round claiming that Jesus never existed, that He was a legend invented later, like the gods of ancient Greece. If you’ve seen one, you might have wondered whether it’s true.

Start with how Luke begins his Gospel. He doesn’t say, “Once upon a time, in a land far away.” He writes like a historian. He knows other people have already written accounts. He has gathered material from “the initial eyewitnesses.” He has “carefully investigated everything from the beginning.” And he’s writing so that his reader may “know the certainty” of what he’s been taught.

Then Luke does something legends never do: he pins his story to dates and names you can check. When John the Baptist begins preaching, Luke dates it like this: “In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, while Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea.” Tiberius and Pilate are not characters from a fairy tale. Tiberius is on Roman coins and in Roman histories. Pilate is named by Roman and Jewish writers, and in 1961 a stone inscription bearing his name was found at Caesarea, on the coast of Israel.

It isn’t only Christians who mention Jesus, either. The Roman historian Tacitus, who had no love for Christians, wrote in the early second century that their name came from “Christus”, who had been executed by Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius. The Jewish historian Josephus, writing in the first century, mentions a man named James, whom he calls “the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ.”

That’s why almost every serious historian, whatever they believe about God, agrees that Jesus of Nazareth really lived, taught in Galilee, gathered followers, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. The question historians argue about isn’t whether He lived. It’s who He was.

And that’s where it gets interesting. Read the Gospels as if for the first time and the Jesus you meet there is not a soft, forgettable religious teacher. He forgives sins as if they were committed against Him personally. He calms storms. He says He will rise from the dead. He is gentle with outcasts and fierce with religious hypocrites. People who met Him walked away amazed, or furious, or worshipping. Almost no one walked away bored.

Luke wanted Theophilus to have certainty, not because Theophilus was told to switch off his brain, but because the facts could bear the weight. The same is true for you. Your faith isn’t floating in mid-air. It’s anchored in history: in a real man, in a real place, at a real time.

So don’t just take someone’s word for who Jesus was, not even this book’s. Read the eyewitness accounts yourself.

Think about it: If you’d never heard of Jesus before and read Luke’s Gospel for the first time, what do you think would surprise you most?

Try this: Start reading Luke’s Gospel today. It has twenty-four chapters, so a chapter a day takes less than a month. Every time Jesus says or does something that surprises you, write it down.

Go deeper: The Everlasting Man by G. K. Chesterton — Chesterton tries to read the Gospels as an outsider seeing them for the first time, and finds that the Jesus there is far stranger and more startling than the mild figure people expect, so strange that only belief makes sense of Him. Start with chapter 12, “The Riddles of the Gospel”.

Lord Jesus, thank You that You really came, into a real place and a real time, and that people saw You, heard You and wrote it down. Help me not to settle for second-hand ideas about You. As I read about You, show me who You really are. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 5 — Did He Really Rise?
fields.body_html:
“For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles. And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth.”

— 1 Corinthians 15:3–8 (BSB)

Everything hangs on this. Paul says so himself, a few verses later: “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile; you are still in your sins.” Christianity doesn’t say “Jesus was a good teacher, so try to be nice.” It says He died and came back to life. If that didn’t happen, the whole thing falls. If it did, everything changes.

So did it happen? Here are four things worth weighing.

The report is early. Paul wrote this letter about twenty-five years after Jesus died, and the words in today’s passage are something he “received” and “passed on”, a summary that was already being handed around. That puts it very close to the events themselves, too close for a legend to grow. And notice the detail: “most of whom are still living.” Paul is practically saying, “Don’t believe me? Go and ask them.”

The tomb was empty. The disciples preached the resurrection in Jerusalem, the very city where Jesus had been buried. If His body had still been in the tomb, His enemies could have ended the whole movement by producing it. Instead, they spread the story that the disciples had stolen the body, which admits the tomb was empty.

The first witnesses were women. In that culture, a woman’s testimony was often not taken seriously, and Luke tells us that even the disciples first thought the women’s report “seemed like nonsense.” If you were inventing a story to convince people, you would never have written it that way. You’d write it that way only if that’s how it happened.

The witnesses were changed. On the night Jesus was arrested, His followers ran. Weeks later, the same people were preaching openly in the city that had crucified Him, and many of them were later beaten, imprisoned and killed rather than take it back. People will die for something they believe is true, but not for something they know they made up. Jesus’ own brother James, who hadn’t believed in Him, became a leader of the church. Paul, who had hunted Christians down, became the greatest missionary the early church ever had.

A stolen body, a hallucination, a case of mistaken identity: each of these explanations runs into one wall or another. The explanation that fits all the facts is the one the witnesses gave. “Christ has indeed been raised from the dead.”

And if He has, then death is not the end, forgiveness is real, and Jesus is not a hero of the past. He is alive now. You can know Him. That’s what the next few days are building towards.

Think about it: Which piece of evidence do you find most convincing? What question do you still have about the resurrection?

Try this: Read one of the resurrection accounts slowly today: Luke 24 or John 20. Imagine you’re one of the people in the story. What would you have felt?

Go deeper: On the Incarnation by Athanasius of Alexandria — writing in the fourth century, Athanasius argues that a dead man doesn’t go on changing people’s lives across the world, so what the risen Christ is still doing is itself evidence that He is alive. Start with chapter 30, “The reality of the resurrection proved by facts”.

Lord Jesus, You died for my sins and You rose again on the third day. Thank You that the tomb is empty and that You are alive. Where I still have questions, keep leading me towards the truth. And because You live, help me not to be afraid of death or of anything else. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 6 — Why Does God Allow Suffering?
fields.body_html:
“I consider that our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us… We know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time.”

— Romans 8:18, 22 (BSB)

A flood sweeps through a village. A friend’s mum is diagnosed with cancer. You scroll past footage of a war and can’t get the faces out of your head. Sooner or later almost everyone asks it: If God is good and powerful, why does He let this happen?

It’s a fair question, and the Bible doesn’t run from it. Whole books of the Bible, like Job and Lamentations, are spent wrestling with it. Christianity doesn’t give a neat answer that makes the pain disappear. But it gives more to hold on to than any other view of the world.

The world is broken, and it knows it. Paul says the whole creation is “groaning”. Things are not the way they were meant to be. The Bible traces that back to humanity turning away from God. Much suffering comes directly from human choices: greed, violence, cruelty. God made us able to love, and love requires real freedom, which means freedom to do real harm. Other suffering, like disease and disaster, comes from living in a world that has been knocked off its axis.

Your outrage points somewhere. When you see injustice and something in you says, This is wrong, you’re measuring the world against a standard of how things ought to be. Where does that standard come from? If there is no God, suffering is just what happens. But you don’t feel that it’s just what happens. You feel it’s wrong, and that feeling fits a world made by a good God and then spoiled.

God didn’t stay out of it. This is the heart of it. God’s answer to suffering is not mainly an explanation. It’s Himself. Standing at the grave of His friend Lazarus, knowing He was about to raise him, “Jesus wept.” Then He went to the cross and took the worst that evil could do. Whatever you’re going through, you’re not praying to a God who has never suffered.

It won’t last forever. Paul had been beaten, shipwrecked and imprisoned, and he still said that “our present sufferings are not comparable to the glory that will be revealed in us.” Groaning, he says, is like the pains of childbirth: real pain, but pain that leads to new life. The Bible ends with God wiping away every tear and death being no more.

And even now, God is not idle. Paul wrote in the same chapter, “God works all things together for the good of those who love Him.” That doesn’t mean bad things are secretly good. It means God can bring good even out of them.

If you’re carrying something heavy right now, a loss or a sadness that won’t lift, please don’t carry it alone. Tell God honestly, and tell a parent or a trusted adult too.

Think about it: Is there a time you’ve seen God bring something good out of something painful, in your life or someone else’s?

Try this: Think of someone you know who is going through a hard time. Pray for them by name today, then send them a short message or do one kind thing for them.

Go deeper: The God of All Comfort by Hannah Whitall Smith — after a life marked by real grief, Smith writes that the simple words “The Lord is good” stopped her short every time appearances tempted her to think God had been unkind or careless. Start with chapter 7, “The Lord is Good”.

God of all comfort, I don’t understand why there is so much pain in the world. Thank You that You aren’t far from it, and that Jesus wept and suffered too. Be close to everyone who is hurting today, especially the people I’m thinking of now. Help me trust that You are good, even when I can’t see it. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 7 — Faith and Science
fields.body_html:
“The heavens declare the glory of God; the skies proclaim the work of His hands. Day after day they pour forth speech; night after night they reveal knowledge. Without speech or language, without a sound to be heard, their voice has gone out into all the earth, their words to the ends of the world.”

— Psalm 19:1–4 (BSB)

Maybe you’ve picked up the idea, from a teacher, a documentary or a comments section, that you have to choose: either science or God. Smart people pick science. People who need comfort pick God.

It’s a popular story. It just isn’t true.

Psalm 19 was written about three thousand years ago by someone looking up at the night sky. He didn’t know about galaxies or light-years. But he knew the sky was saying something. Day after day, it says, they “pour forth speech.” Every star is a word about the One who made it.

Think about what science actually does. It asks how the universe works: how cells divide, how stars burn, how a virus spreads. Those are wonderful questions. But there are other questions science isn’t designed to answer. Why is there a universe at all? Why does it run on laws we can understand? What is a human life for? Imagine explaining a song by measuring its sound waves. You’d learn something true, but you’d miss why the composer wrote it.

Modern science actually grew up among people who believed in a Creator. They expected the universe to be orderly because it had a lawgiver, and they expected to be able to understand it because they were made in the image of a reasoning God. That tradition didn’t end long ago. The scientist who first proposed that the universe began from a tiny, dense starting point, the idea now called the Big Bang, was Georges Lemaître, a Belgian physicist who was also a Catholic priest. Francis Collins, who led the international project to map human DNA, was an atheist until his twenties, when he started reading C. S. Lewis and became a Christian.

That doesn’t mean every question is easy. Christians who love God and respect science sometimes disagree, for example about how to read the opening chapters of Genesis. That’s fine. Those debates are worth having, and they don’t touch the centre of the faith: that God made all things, and that Jesus died and rose again.

So don’t be afraid of your science lessons. Study hard. Ask questions. Every true thing you learn about how the world works is something true about how God made it. The Bible even says, “It is the glory of God to conceal a matter and the glory of kings to search it out.” Discovery is a kind of treasure hunt God set up on purpose.

The heavens are still declaring. The more you understand them, the more there is to hear.

Think about it: Have you ever felt that believing in God and loving science don’t fit together? What would change if you saw science as studying what God made?

Try this: Tonight, look at the sky for a few minutes. Or look up one amazing fact about the universe or the human body. Then thank God for it.

Go deeper: The Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis — explains Lewis’s argument in Miracles that if nature were all there is, we’d have no reason to trust our own reasoning, and that the laws of nature describe the world God made rather than forbid Him to act in it. Start with chapter 15, “The Grand Miracle”.

Creator God, the heavens declare Your glory, and the more we learn, the more there is to wonder at. Thank You for my mind and for the chance to study Your world. Keep me curious and honest, and let every true thing I learn lead me back to worship You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 8 — Is Jesus the Only Way?
fields.body_html:
“Salvation exists in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to men by which we must be saved.”

— Acts 4:12 (BSB)

Your classmates might be Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, Sikh or nothing in particular. Some of them are kinder than some Christians you know. So when Christians say Jesus is the only way to God, it can sound narrow, even arrogant. How can one religion be right and all the others wrong?

Start with this: Christians didn’t invent the claim. Jesus made it. “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through Me.” And Peter repeated it in today’s verse, standing in front of the very leaders who had just had Jesus killed. That wasn’t arrogance. It was risky.

Here’s why it isn’t as narrow as it sounds. Most religions are, at heart, a path up: rules, practices and good deeds by which people try to reach God. Christianity says something different. Our problem isn’t that we lack good teaching. It’s that we’ve turned away from God, and we can’t climb back. The Bible puts it bluntly: “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” So God came down. Jesus, God the Son, lived the life we haven’t, and died the death we deserved. “God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

If that’s true, then Jesus isn’t one teacher among many. He’s the only one who dealt with sin by taking it on Himself, and the only one who walked out of His own grave. As D. L. Moody put it, Jesus is either an impostor or He is who He said He was. There isn’t much room in between.

And the door is open to everyone. Anyone from any country, any background, any religion, can come. “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

That should make Christians the most respectful people around, not the most arrogant. We didn’t earn anything. We should treat our neighbours of other faiths with “gentleness and respect”, listen to them carefully, and be honest about why we follow Jesus.

Now the most personal question in this book: have you trusted Jesus for yourself? Not your parents’ faith, not your church’s, but yours?

It isn’t complicated. Admit to God that you’ve sinned and can’t fix it yourself. Believe that Jesus died for you and rose again. And receive Him: “to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God.” If you’re ready, you could pray something like this, in your own words: Jesus, I’ve gone my own way. I believe You died for my sins and rose again. I trust You now as my Saviour and my Lord. Make me Yours.

If you prayed that and meant it, tell a Christian you trust today. And if you’re not ready yet, that’s honest. Keep seeking. He isn’t going anywhere.

Think about it: What makes Jesus different from every other religious teacher you know of? Is there anything holding you back from trusting Him?

Try this: If you trusted Christ today, tell a parent, a youth leader or a Christian friend. If you’re not ready, write down what’s stopping you, and talk to someone about it this week.

Go deeper: The Way to God by Dwight L. Moody — Moody tells how, as a boy, he thought Jesus was simply the best man who ever lived, until he faced Jesus’ own claims and concluded He must be either a deceiver or God come in the flesh. Start with chapter 5, “A Divine Saviour”.

Lord Jesus, You are the way and the truth and the life. Thank You that You came down to find me when I couldn’t climb up to God. I trust You as my Saviour and give You my life as my Lord. Help me to treat everyone with gentleness and respect, and to be ready to tell them why I hope in You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 9 — When God Feels Silent
fields.body_html:
“How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? How long must I wrestle in my soul, with sorrow in my heart each day? How long will my enemy dominate me?… But I have trusted in Your loving devotion; my heart will rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.”

— Psalm 13:1–2, 5–6 (BSB)

You pray, and it feels like talking to the ceiling. You open the Bible, and the words lie flat on the page. Other people at church seem to sense God everywhere, and you sense nothing at all. You start to wonder whether God has gone quiet, or whether He was ever there.

If that’s you, look at Psalm 13. David, the man the Bible calls a man after God’s own heart, says “How long?” four times in two verses. Have You forgotten me? Are You hiding from me? That’s not a polite prayer. It’s raw. And God put it in the Bible.

That alone tells you something important. Feeling far from God doesn’t mean you’ve failed, and it isn’t a sign that God has left. Some of the most faithful people in Scripture felt exactly the same. Jesus Himself, on the cross, cried out, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” Honest complaint to God is still prayer. In fact, it’s a kind of faith: you don’t shout “How long?” at someone you believe isn’t there.

Now watch what happens in the last two verses. Nothing in David’s situation has obviously changed. But something shifts: “But I have trusted in Your loving devotion.” David turns from what he feels to what he knows. He remembers who God is and what God has done: “He has been good to me.” Feelings are real, but they’re not the whole story. God’s love didn’t stop being true just because David couldn’t feel it.

So what do you do in a silent season?

  • Keep showing up. Keep reading, keep praying, even if it feels dry. A seed underground looks like nothing is happening for a long time.
  • Be honest. Tell God exactly how it feels. He can take it.
  • Remember. Write down times God has been faithful to you before. Read them on the dry days.
  • Lean on others. Let other Christians carry you a little. Faith isn’t a solo sport.

John Bunyan, who later wrote The Pilgrim’s Progress, went through years of fear and darkness when he was sure God had shut him out. Then, as he sat among other believers one day, the words “My grace is sufficient for you” came home to his heart with such force that they changed everything.

One more thing. Sometimes feeling far from God is mixed up with a sadness that just won’t lift. If that heaviness lasts, or if you ever think about hurting yourself or not wanting to be alive, please tell a parent or a trusted adult right away. That isn’t weakness, and it isn’t a lack of faith. It’s exactly what God wants you to do.

Think about it: Have you ever felt that God was silent? What helped, or what do you think might help?

Try this: Write your own “How long?” prayer, telling God honestly how you feel. Then finish it the way David did, with one thing you know is true about God, even if you don’t feel it.

Go deeper: Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners by John Bunyan — Bunyan’s own story of long months when he feared no word of God could help him, until “My grace is sufficient” broke through, at first in part and then in full. Start with chapter 3, “Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners; Or, a Brief Relation of the Exceeding Mercy of God in Christ, to His Poor Servant John Bunyan”.

Lord, sometimes it feels like You’re far away and I can’t hear You at all. How long? I’m telling You honestly how it feels. But I choose to trust in Your loving devotion, because You have been good to me. Hold on to me, even when I can’t feel You holding on. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 10 — Faith Is Not a Feeling
fields.body_html:
“Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.”

— Hebrews 11:1 (BSB)

You come home from a camp or a conference, and God feels so close you could almost touch Him. Then Monday comes. School, chores, an argument at home, a message that stings. By Wednesday, the feeling is gone. And a worrying thought creeps in: Was any of it real?

Here’s something that might set you free: faith is not a feeling.

Hebrews says faith is “the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see.” Notice those words: assurance and certainty. Faith isn’t a warm glow, and it isn’t a leap in the dark. It’s trust, resting your weight on something you have good reason to believe, even when you can’t see it.

You do this all the time. When you sit on a chair, you don’t first check how you feel about the chair. You have good reason to think it’ll hold you, so you sit. When you cross a bridge over a river, you aren’t relying on your mood. You’re relying on the bridge.

That’s what these ten days have been about. You’ve looked at reasons to believe that God exists, that the Bible can be trusted, that Jesus really lived, and that He really rose. Faith is what happens when you stop standing next to the chair, examining it, and sit down.

Feelings are like the weather. They change with sleep, hormones, exams, friendships and a hundred other things. Some days you’ll feel close to God. Some days you won’t feel anything. That’s normal. Feelings are a gift from God, but they make a terrible anchor. Remember Hebrews 6:19: our hope is “an anchor for the soul, firm and secure” because it’s fastened to Jesus, not to how we feel about Him on a given day. “We walk by faith, not by sight.”

Hannah Whitall Smith once described a clever young man who was trapped by doubt. Nothing felt real to him, and the harder he tried to feel it, the less real it seemed. Someone told him he didn’t have to control his feelings. He only had to decide which side his will was on. So he said, in effect, I choose to believe. I will believe. I do believe. His feelings kept protesting for a while, and he kept choosing. In the end, his feelings caught up. His life became, she said, one of the finest Christian lives she knew.

That’s not pretending. It’s what the father in Mark 9 did on Day 1: “I do believe; help my unbelief!” Faith is choosing to trust God with your life because He has shown He can be trusted, and then letting Him deal with your feelings in His own time.

So on the days you feel nothing, don’t panic. Keep trusting. The anchor holds whether you can feel it or not.

Think about it: Have you ever judged your relationship with God by how you felt? What would change if you judged it by what God has said and done?

Try this: Write three things you know are true about God, whatever you feel today. Put them somewhere you’ll see them on a day when God feels far away.

Go deeper: The Christian’s Secret of a Happy Life by Hannah Whitall Smith — Smith shows that the Christian life is lived in the will, not the emotions, and tells of a young man who overcame years of doubt by simply putting his will on the believing side. Start with chapter 7, “Difficulties Concerning the Will”.

Father, thank You that my relationship with You doesn’t rise and fall with my feelings. On the days I feel close to You and on the days I feel nothing, I choose to trust You. You are faithful, and Your Word is true. Anchor me in You, firm and secure. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 11 — Made in His Image
fields.body_html:
“When I behold Your heavens, the work of Your fingers, the moon and the stars, which You have set in place—what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor.”

— Psalm 8:3–5 (BSB)

Go somewhere dark one night, away from the streetlights, and look up. The longer you look, the more stars appear, and the smaller you start to feel. Some of that light left its star before your great-grandparents were born. You are one person on one planet, circling one ordinary star, in a galaxy of billions.

David felt exactly that. He looked up and asked the question every thinking person eventually asks: Why would the God who made all that pay attention to someone like me?

There are two easy answers, and both are wrong. One says you are nothing: a lucky arrangement of atoms, here for a while and then gone, so nothing you do really matters. The other says you are everything: the centre of your own story, free to define yourself however you like, answerable to nobody. Plenty of people swing between the two in a single week. On a good day you’re the main character; on a bad day you’re nobody.

The Bible gives a better answer, and it starts on the first page: “So God created man in His own image; in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them.” To be made in God’s image means you were made to reflect Him: to think, to create, to love, to choose, to rule over the world with care, and above all to know Him. A mirror isn’t valuable because of what it is in itself. It’s valuable because of what it shows.

That changes how you see yourself. Your worth isn’t something you earn with marks, followers or a starting place on the team. It was given to you before you did anything at all. And because it was given, nobody can vote it away. Not the person who laughed at you, not the group chat that left you out, not even you on your worst day.

It also changes how you see everyone else. James points out how strange it is that “with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.” The classmate you find annoying, the refugee family down the road, the cleaner nobody greets: every one of them carries the image of God. You can’t honour God and treat His image with contempt.

The image has been damaged. Sin has scratched and cracked the mirror, and you know that from the inside. That’s why the New Testament speaks of being renewed into the likeness of Jesus, who is the perfect image of God. Becoming more like Him isn’t becoming less yourself. It’s becoming what you were made to be.

Sixteen centuries ago a restless young man in North Africa tried everything to fill the emptiness inside him. Later he prayed: “Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.” You were made in God’s image, and for Him.

Think about it: Do you tend to think of yourself as “nothing” or as “everything”? What would change if you saw yourself as an image-bearer instead?

Try this: Pick one person today you usually overlook or find irritating. Remind yourself silently, made in God’s image, and treat them that way.

Go deeper: Confessions by Augustine — the most famous autobiography in Christian history opens with a young man discovering that his restlessness was really a hunger for God. Start with chapter 1, “Book I.”

Creator God, when I look at the size of everything You made, I wonder why You notice me. Thank You that You made me in Your image and gave me a worth no one can take away. Where sin has cracked that image, make me more like Jesus. Help me see that same image in every person I meet today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 12 — Known Completely
fields.body_html:
“O LORD, You have searched me and known me. You know when I sit and when I rise; You understand my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down; You are aware of all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, You know all about it, O LORD.”

— Psalm 139:1–4 (BSB)

Imagine your phone’s entire history being projected onto a screen at school assembly. Every search. Every message you typed and deleted. Every photo, every private note, every thought you had about the people in the room. Most of us would rather disappear.

Now read David’s words again. God knows all of it, and more. Not just what you did, but when you sit and when you rise, the thoughts behind your face, the word before it reaches your tongue. That can sound terrifying. “Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight; everything is uncovered and exposed.”

But notice David’s tone. He isn’t panicking. He’s amazed: “Such knowledge is too wonderful for me.” Why?

Because there’s a deep fear underneath most of our lives: If people really knew me, they wouldn’t want me. So we curate. We show the version of ourselves that gets approved, and we hide the rest. That’s exhausting. And it means that even when people love us, a voice whispers, They only love the version they’ve seen.

God is the one person you can’t curate for. He has already seen everything: the worst thing you’ve done, the thought you’d never say aloud, the fear you can’t name. And here’s the astonishing thing. Knowing all of it, He did not turn away. “But God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” He didn’t love a cleaned-up version of you. He loved the real one, enough to die for it.

That means you are known and loved, which is what every human heart actually wants. To be loved but not known feels fake. To be known but not loved is the stuff of nightmares. To be fully known and fully loved is freedom.

Long before David, a runaway servant girl named Hagar sat alone by a spring in the desert, pregnant, mistreated and unseen by anyone who mattered. God met her there, and she gave Him a name: “You are the God who sees me.” She was nobody to the world. She wasn’t nobody to Him.

So you don’t have to perform for God. You can stop pretending in prayer. You can tell Him what’s actually going on, because He already knows, and He’s still listening. David ends the psalm by inviting God to look even closer: “Search me, O God, and know my heart.” That’s not the prayer of someone hiding. It’s the prayer of someone who has realised there’s nowhere safer to be seen.

Think about it: Is there a part of your life you’ve been trying to keep hidden, even from God? What would it be like to stop?

Try this: Pray Psalm 139:23–24 out loud tonight, slowly, and then sit in silence for one full minute. Tell God one honest thing you usually leave out.

fields.title: Day 13 — The Real You and Your Feed
fields.body_html:
“How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?”

— John 5:44 (BSB)

You post a photo. Then you check. Ten minutes later you check again. Someone you thought was a friend hasn’t liked it. Someone you don’t even know has. By the evening you have a number, and somehow that number has become a verdict on you.

None of this is new. Jesus said these words to religious leaders long before phones existed. They lived for “glory from one another”: the respect of the crowd, the best seats, the admiring nods. Jesus said that hunger made it almost impossible for them to believe. When you’re constantly looking sideways at what people think, it’s very hard to look up at what God thinks.

Your feed works on the same hunger. It rewards the angle, the filter, the best ten seconds of the day. Over time, without meaning to, you start building a second self: the one online who is always fine, always funny, always somewhere interesting. Then you start to feel you have to protect that person. And the real you, the one who is tired, unsure, sometimes lonely, starts to feel like a fraud.

A. W. Tozer called this “the burden of pretense”: “the common human desire to put the best foot forward and hide from the world our real inward poverty.” He said hardly anyone dares to be just what they are “without doctoring up the impression.” He wrote that in 1948. He would recognise your timeline instantly.

Paul faced the same choice and settled it: “Am I now seeking the approval of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? If I were still trying to please men, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

Here’s the freedom in that. People’s approval is a moving target. It changes with the algorithm and the mood of the group chat. God’s verdict on those who belong to Jesus does not change: “your life is now hidden with Christ in God.” Hidden, not displayed. Safe, not on show. You don’t have to win it again tomorrow.

This doesn’t mean you have to delete everything. Phones aren’t evil, and sharing life with friends is good. The question is who you’re performing for. Are you posting to share something, or to be told you’re worth something? Are you being honest, or building a mask that you then have to wear?

Try asking that before you post. Better still, try living some of your best moments with no audience at all. A kindness nobody films. A prayer nobody sees. Jesus said your Father “sees what is done in secret.” There’s a whole life you can live just for Him, and it turns out to be the one where you feel most like yourself.

Think about it: How different is the “you” on your phone from the you that your family sees at home? Which one feels more tiring?

Try this: For one day, before you post anything, ask: Am I sharing, or am I asking to be approved? If it’s the second, wait. Notice how it feels.

Go deeper: The Pursuit of God by A. W. Tozer — Tozer describes the exhausting burdens of pride and pretense, and the rest that comes when we accept God’s estimate of us and stop caring about the world’s. Start with chapter 11, “Meekness and Rest.”

Father, I admit I care a lot about what people think of me. I’ve built masks I’m tired of wearing. Help me seek the glory that comes from You, not the approval of the crowd. Let my real life be hidden with Christ, safe in You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 14 — The Comparison Trap
fields.body_html:
“We do not dare to classify or compare ourselves with some who commend themselves. When they measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves with themselves, they show their ignorance.”

— 2 Corinthians 10:12 (BSB)

Exam results come out. You did well, better than you expected, and for about four minutes you’re happy. Then you see a friend’s grades. They did better. Suddenly your good result feels like failure.

Comparison is a strange thief. It doesn’t take what you have; it just makes you unable to enjoy it. It works in every direction. Compare yourself with someone “ahead” and you feel jealous or worthless. Compare yourself with someone “behind” and you feel quietly proud. Either way, you’re measuring your life with someone else’s ruler.

Paul was writing to a church where some teachers had set themselves up as the standard. They measured themselves against each other and came out looking impressive. Paul’s verdict was blunt: that isn’t wisdom, it’s ignorance. A few verses later he says why: “For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.” Only one opinion of your life finally counts, and it isn’t your classmates’, your cousins’ or even your own.

Comparison feels natural because it’s built into school, sport and social media: rankings, positions, followers. Some of that is fine. A race needs a winner. But when ranking becomes the way you decide what you’re worth, you’ll never rest. There’s always someone cleverer, faster, better-looking, more liked. And the moment you overtake them, a new name appears.

Jesus once restored Peter and gave him a calling. Within seconds Peter pointed at John and asked, “Lord, what about him?” Jesus’ reply was almost sharp: “what is that to you? You follow Me!” Your path is yours. God hasn’t asked you to run your friend’s race.

Andrew Murray, writing about humility, describes someone who has met God and is set free from all this. That person “no longer compares itself with others.” He “feels no jealousy or envy” and “can praise God when others are preferred and blessed before him.” That isn’t low self-esteem. It’s the relief of no longer needing to win.

So how do you escape the trap? Three things help.

First, thank God for what you’ve been given before you look sideways. Gratitude and envy struggle to live in the same heart.

Second, celebrate someone else on purpose. When a friend wins, tell them you’re glad, and mean it. It’s surprisingly freeing, and it weakens jealousy’s grip every time you do it.

Third, remember the only verdict that lasts. You are not the sum of your rankings. If you belong to Jesus, God has already said what He thinks of you, and that does not go up and down with the results list.

Think about it: Who do you compare yourself with most often? What does that comparison usually do to you?

Try this: Message one person today to congratulate them on something they did well, especially someone you’ve felt jealous of.

Go deeper: Humility by Andrew Murray — Murray argues that real humility shows up not in prayers but in daily life with other people, where the humble heart “no longer compares itself with others” and can rejoice when someone else is praised. Start with chapter 6, “Humility in Daily Life.”

Lord, I keep measuring myself by other people, and it steals my joy. Forgive me for envy and for quiet pride. Help me thank You for what You’ve given me, and celebrate others when they do well. Let Your opinion of me be the one that matters most. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 15 — When You’ve Blown It
fields.body_html:
“Simon, Simon, Satan has asked to sift each of you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, Simon, that your faith will not fail. And when you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”

— Luke 22:31–32 (BSB)

There’s a particular feeling after you’ve really messed up. Maybe you lied to your parents and got caught. Maybe you said something cruel and it was screenshotted. Maybe you did the thing you promised God you’d never do again. Your stomach drops. A voice in your head says, That’s who you really are. God’s finished with you now.

Peter knew that feeling better than anyone.

On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter swore he would never leave Him: “Lord, I am ready to go with You even to prison and to death.” A few hours later, standing by a fire, he denied even knowing Jesus. Three times. Then the rooster crowed, and Luke records one of the most painful sentences in the Bible: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.” Peter “went outside and wept bitterly.”

But read today’s verses again. Before any of it happened, Jesus already knew. And He had already prayed for him. Notice what He didn’t say. He didn’t say, “If you fail, you’re finished.” He said, “when you have turned back.” Jesus expected Peter to fall, and He was already planning his return. He even had a job waiting: “strengthen your brothers.”

After the resurrection, the angel at the tomb gave the women a message: “go, tell His disciples and Peter.” Peter was named on purpose. Then, beside another fire on a beach, Jesus asked him three times, “Do you love Me?” One question for each denial. Not to shame him, but to heal him. Peter went on to preach to thousands.

There’s a difference between guilt that crushes and guilt that leads home. The first says, You are a failure. Hide. That’s the voice of the accuser, and its aim is to keep you away from God. The second says, You did wrong. Go back. That’s the Holy Spirit, and His aim is always to bring you to Jesus. Peter wept bitterly, but he didn’t run off for good. He came back.

So when you’ve blown it, do what Peter eventually did. Be honest about it. Don’t shrink it or blame someone else. “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” If you’ve hurt someone, put it right with them as far as you can. And then, believe you are forgiven. Refusing to accept forgiveness can look humble, but it’s actually saying Jesus’ death wasn’t quite enough.

Isaiah described the Messiah this way, and Matthew applied it to Jesus: “A bruised reed He will not break, and a smoldering wick He will not extinguish.” If you feel bent and barely glowing today, you’re exactly the kind of person He’s gentle with.

Think about it: When you fail, which voice do you usually listen to: hide or go back? Why?

Try this: If there’s something you’ve been carrying, confess it to God today in plain words. If it involved someone else, decide when you’ll go and make it right.

Go deeper: The Bruised Reed by Richard Sibbes — a 400-year-old book written for people who feel weak, guilty and close to giving up, showing that Jesus “never turned any back again that came unto him.” Start with chapter 3, “Christ will not break the Bruised Reed.”

Lord Jesus, You know where I’ve failed, and You knew before I did it. Thank You that You pray for me and that You haven’t given up on me. I confess what I’ve done, and I trust that Your death is enough to forgive it. Help me turn back, and then use me to strengthen others. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 16 — Anxious
fields.body_html:
“You will keep in perfect peace the steadfast of mind, because he trusts in You. Trust in the LORD forever, because GOD the LORD is the Rock eternal.”

— Isaiah 26:3–4 (BSB)

It’s 1 a.m. and your mind won’t stop. The exam on Thursday. The thing you said that might have upset a friend. Your parents arguing about money. Something you saw in the news. Your heart is racing, your chest feels tight, and the more you tell yourself to calm down, the worse it gets.

If that sounds familiar, you’re not strange, and you’re not a bad Christian. Anxiety is one of the most common struggles for people your age, all over the world. Some people feel it as worry that won’t switch off. Others feel it in their body: a churning stomach, shaky hands, trouble breathing. The Bible doesn’t pretend God’s people never feel this. David wrote psalms in the middle of it. Jesus Himself, the night before the cross, said, “My soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death.”

So what does God offer? Not a switch that makes every feeling disappear, but a Rock to stand on while the waves hit.

Isaiah talks about a mind that is “steadfast,” literally a mind that leans on something. Peace doesn’t come from controlling every outcome. You can’t. It comes from leaning your weight on the One who does: “the Rock eternal.” Your exam result might shift; your friendships might shift; even your family situation might shift. He doesn’t.

Paul gives a practical shape to that leaning: “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.” That’s not “stop feeling anxious or else.” It’s an invitation. Take each worry, one at a time, and hand it over by name. Peter says the same: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.” You’re not bothering Him.

Some simple things genuinely help too, and using them isn’t a lack of faith. Breathe slowly. Get enough sleep, which may mean putting the phone in another room at night. Move your body. Write your worries down so your brain can stop holding them. Pray a short verse over and over when your thoughts are spinning: You are the Rock eternal.

And here’s something important. Talk to someone. Anxiety grows in secret and shrinks when it’s shared. A parent, an older Christian you trust, a teacher, a youth leader. If the worry or fear lasts for weeks, if it stops you from sleeping, eating or going to school, or if you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself or of not wanting to be alive, tell a parent or trusted adult right away. That isn’t weakness, and it isn’t a failure of faith. Getting help, including from a doctor or counsellor, is one of the ways God cares for you.

You don’t have to feel calm to be held. The Rock holds you even when your hands are shaking.

Think about it: What does anxiety feel like for you? Who is one person you could tell when it gets heavy?

Try this: Tonight, write down every worry on your mind. Then go through the list and pray over each one by name: “Lord, I’m handing You this.” Leave the paper on the table, not under your pillow.

Go deeper: The Life of Trust (For Teens), from the journals of George Müller — in a season when he had no idea how a hundred children would eat that evening, Müller didn’t fake peace; he brought God specific, honest requests and kept doing the next right thing. Start with chapter 9, “Almost by the Hour.”

Lord, You know how anxious I feel, even the worries I can’t explain. I hand them to You one by one, because You care for me. Be my Rock when everything else feels shaky. Give me courage to tell someone when I’m struggling, and keep my mind steady on You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Take each worry, one at a time, and hand it over by name. Peter says the same: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.” You’re not bothering Him. Some simple things genuinely help too, and using them isn’t a lack of faith. Breathe slowly. Get enough sleep, which may mean putting the phone in another room at night. Move your body. Write your worries down so your brain can stop holding them. Pray a short verse over and over when your thoughts are spinning: You are the Rock eternal. And here’s something important. Talk to someone. Anxiety grows in secret and shrinks when it’s shared. A parent, an older Christian you trust, a teacher, a youth leader. If the worry or fear lasts for weeks, if it stops you from sleeping, eating or going to school, or if you ever have thoughts of hurting yourself or of not wanting to be alive, tell a parent or trusted adult right away. That isn’t weakness, and it isn’t a failure of faith. Getting help, including from a doctor or counsellor, is one of the ways God cares for you. You don’t have to feel calm to be held. The Rock holds you even when your hands are shaking. Think about it: What does anxiety feel like for you? Who is one person you could tell when it gets heavy? Try this: Tonight, write down every worry on your mind. Then go through the list and pray over each one by name: “Lord, I’m handing You this.” Leave the paper on the table, not under your pillow. Start with chapter 9, “Almost by the Hour.” Lord, You know how anxious I feel, even the worries I can’t explain. I hand them to You one by one, because You care for me. fields.title: Day 17 — Lonely
fields.body_html:
“Turn to me and be gracious, for I am lonely and afflicted. The troubles of my heart increase; free me from my distress.”

— Psalm 25:16–17 (BSB)

You can be lonely in a crowded classroom. You can be lonely in a busy house. You can be lonely with three hundred contacts in your phone. Loneliness isn’t just being alone. It’s the feeling that nobody really sees you, or that if you disappeared for a week, it might take a while for anyone to notice.

Maybe your best friend has found a new group and you’re on the edge of it. Maybe your family moved to a new city, or a new country, and you’re the new one who doesn’t know the language of the playground jokes. Maybe you’re the only Christian in your class. Maybe there’s just a quiet ache you can’t explain.

Look at today’s prayer. David, the king, the warrior, the songwriter, said plainly: “I am lonely.” He didn’t dress it up. He didn’t pretend to feel close to God in that moment. He just told God the truth and asked Him to turn toward him. That is a prayer you are allowed to pray.

Loneliness isn’t a sign that God has abandoned you. Jesus knew it from the inside. On the night of His arrest, the disciples He’d poured His life into ran: “Then everyone deserted Him and fled.” But Jesus had said beforehand, “you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me.” And He made a promise to everyone who follows Him: “And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

Always. On the bus, at lunch when you don’t know where to sit, at 2 a.m. when nobody’s online.

A cook in a French monastery in the 1600s, Brother Lawrence, learned to live in that promise. He worked in a hot, noisy kitchen, did jobs nobody noticed, and described himself as a “great awkward fellow who broke everything.” But he learned to talk with God all day long, among the pots and pans, as you’d talk with a friend in the room. He found that God was never far away.

God’s presence doesn’t mean you don’t need people. You do. God made you for friendship. So while you lean on Him, take small brave steps toward others. Sit next to someone else who looks alone. Join something: a church youth group, a choir, a team, a club. Ask a question and actually listen to the answer. Often the people around you are lonelier than they look.

And if loneliness sits on you heavily for a long time, or starts turning into deep sadness or thoughts that you don’t want to be alive, tell a parent or trusted adult right away. You don’t have to carry it by yourself.

Think about it: When do you feel most lonely? What would it look like to talk to God in that exact moment?

Try this: Today, find one person who looks like they’re on the edge, and include them. And at three random moments today, say quietly, “Lord, You’re here.”

Go deeper: The Practice of the Presence of God by Brother Lawrence — a humble monastery cook explains how he learned to keep up a constant, simple conversation with God, even in the middle of ordinary work. Start with chapter 1, “First Conversation.”

Lord, sometimes I feel so alone. Turn to me and be gracious. Thank You that Jesus knew loneliness, and that He promised to be with me always. Help me notice You with me today, and give me courage to reach out to others who feel alone too. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 18 — You Belong Somewhere
fields.body_html:
“Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household… And in Him you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.”

— Ephesians 2:19, 22 (BSB)

Think about how it feels to walk into a room where you don’t belong. A party where you don’t know anyone. A new school mid-year. A family gathering on the side you rarely see. You hover near the door, check your phone, and wait to be noticed or to be allowed to leave.

Paul was writing to people who knew that feeling deeply. Most of them weren’t Jewish. For centuries, people like them had been outsiders to God’s people, kept at a distance. Now Paul tells them: not anymore. Through Jesus, you are “no longer strangers and foreigners.” You are citizens. You are family: “members of God’s household.”

That’s what it means to follow Jesus. Your faith is personal, but it was never meant to be private. When God brings you to Himself, He also brings you into a people. Some of them speak your language and some don’t. Some are your age and some are eighty. Some sing loud songs with drums; some sit quietly in old wooden pews. All over the world, in house churches and stadiums, villages and cities, God is building one family.

Paul’s picture is a building. Every believer is a stone, fitted together with others, so that the whole thing becomes “a dwelling place for God.” A single brick on its own isn’t a house. It needs the others, and they need it.

Many teenagers drift from church around your age. Sometimes there are real reasons: it can feel boring, or nobody talks to you, or the adults seem fake. Those things are worth being honest about. But walking away from God’s people because they aren’t perfect is like leaving your family because they’re annoying at dinner. The church is full of forgiven people who are still being rebuilt, just like you.

Hebrews says it plainly: “Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit, but let us encourage one another.” You don’t just go to church to receive something. You go because someone there needs you. The quiet kid in the youth group. The grandmother who prays for the young people by name. The new family who doesn’t know anyone yet. “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need you.’”

If your church has hardly anyone your age, you can still belong there. Help with the children, sit with the older people, ask them how they came to faith. And if you can’t find a church at all, ask a Christian you trust to help you look. God never meant you to follow Jesus alone.

You walked in as a stranger. You’ve been given a seat at the table.

Think about it: What makes it hard for you to feel you belong at church? What could you bring that others might need?

Try this: This week, introduce yourself to one person at church you’ve never really talked to, someone much older or much younger than you.

Go deeper: The Body of Christ (For Teens), from Watchman Nee — the moment God’s life enters you, you are joined to everyone else who carries that life, because salvation is personal “but never private.” Start with chapter 2, “The Consciousness of the Body of Christ.”

Father, thank You that I’m not a stranger to You anymore. Thank You for making me part of Your family all over the world. When church feels hard, help me stay, and help me see who there needs me. Build me together with Your people into a home for You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 19 — Adopted
fields.body_html:
“For you did not receive a spirit of slavery that returns you to fear, but you received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’ The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.”

— Romans 8:15–16 (BSB)

In the Roman world Paul lived in, adoption was a serious legal act. A wealthy man with no heir might adopt a young man and give him everything: a new name, a new family, full rights of inheritance. All the old debts were cancelled. Legally, he had become a new person. He wasn’t a guest in the house. He was a son.

Paul takes that picture and says: this is what God has done for you in Christ. The word your Bible translates “sonship” means exactly that, being placed into the family with full rights. And this applies to sons and daughters. Elsewhere Paul says God “predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ.” John says that to those who receive Jesus, God “gave the right to become children of God.”

Notice the contrast in today’s verse. There are two ways of relating to God. One is like a slave: always anxious, always trying to earn your place, never sure if you’ve done enough, afraid of being thrown out. The other is like a child who knows they’re wanted. Many people who go to church still live like slaves. They obey because they’re scared, pray because they feel they have to, and wonder whether God is secretly disappointed.

Paul says that’s not your spirit anymore. God’s Spirit lives in you and teaches you a new word: “Abba.” It’s the word a child used for their father, warm and close. Jesus used it when He prayed. Now, through Him, you can too.

Maybe the word “father” is complicated for you. Maybe your dad is absent, or harsh, or you’ve never known him. Maybe you have a great dad, but he’s human and he’s let you down. Families look very different, and if anyone at home makes you feel unsafe, please tell a trusted adult. But hear this: God is not a bigger version of the father you have or haven’t had. He is the Father all fathers were meant to point to. He doesn’t leave. He doesn’t lose His temper. He doesn’t love you less when you fail.

Adoption also tells you who you are. You’re not a project God is tolerating. You’re not an employee on probation. You’re a child, with a name and an inheritance: “So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God.”

And the Spirit Himself “testifies with our spirit that we are God’s children.” On the days you don’t feel it, the truth still stands. On the days you do, that warmth in your heart when you pray, that sense of home, is God’s own voice saying, You’re Mine.

Think about it: Do you relate to God more like a nervous servant or a loved child? What makes you feel that way?

Try this: Start your prayers today with the words “Father, thank You that I’m Your child,” and say it slowly, as if it’s true. Because it is.

Go deeper: The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit by R. A. Torrey — Torrey explains how the Holy Spirit takes us from fearful, formal prayers to a childlike trust that cries “Abba, Father.” Start with chapter 15, “The Holy Spirit Bearing Witness to Our Sonship.”

Abba, Father, thank You for adopting me into Your family through Jesus. Thank You that I’m not a slave who has to earn my place, but Your child. Where I’ve been afraid of You, let Your Spirit remind me that I’m loved. Thank You that You will never leave me. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
