fields.title: Day 20 — Grace, Not Grades
fields.body_html:
“Now the wages of the worker are not credited as a gift, but as an obligation. However, to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked, his faith is credited as righteousness.”

— Romans 4:4–5 (BSB)

Almost everything in your life runs on a simple rule: you get what you earn. Study hard and you pass. Train and you make the team. Work and you get paid. Mess up and you lose privileges. In many places, a single national exam can decide which school you go to next, what you can study and what kind of job you’ll have. No wonder so many teenagers carry a constant pressure: I have to perform, or I’m nothing.

Paul says that’s exactly how wages work. When you’re paid for a job, it’s not a gift; it’s what you’re owed. Nobody thanks their employer for a salary as if it were a surprise present.

Then Paul turns everything upside down. With God, salvation doesn’t work like wages. It’s credited “to the one who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the wicked.” Read that last phrase again. Not “justifies the good,” or “justifies the ones who try really hard.” God justifies the wicked. He declares people right with Himself who have no right to be declared anything.

That sounds almost scandalous. Charles Spurgeon thought so too. He said that people naturally assume that “salvation was for the good,” and he never stopped being amazed that it was the other way round. Jesus “comes, not because we are just, but to make us so.”

This matters because many Christians still secretly live by grades. They know they were saved by grace, but they think they stay loved by performance. Good week, devotions every day: God must be pleased. Bad week, missed prayer, snapped at your sister: God must be cold. That’s not grace. “And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.”

Grace doesn’t mean effort is pointless. Paul also says we are “God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works.” You should still study hard, train hard and work hard. But now you do it from acceptance, not for acceptance. Your effort becomes thank-you, not payment. And a failed exam, a lost match or a rejection letter can hurt without destroying you, because none of them was ever your foundation.

For ten days we’ve asked, Who am I? Here’s the answer God gives. You are made in His image. Fully known. Not defined by your feed or your rank. Forgiven when you fall. Held when you’re anxious. Never truly alone. Part of a family. Adopted as His child. And all of it is a gift. You didn’t earn it. You can’t lose it by a bad grade. You can only receive it, and say thank you.

Think about it: Where do you feel most pressure to perform? How would knowing you’re already accepted change the way you approach it?

Try this: Write on a card: “Accepted by grace, not by grades.” Put it where you study or where you’ll see it before your next big test.

Go deeper: All of Grace by Charles Spurgeon — Spurgeon builds a whole chapter on today’s verse and its “very wonderful words,” that God justifies the ungodly. Start with chapter 3, “God Justifieth the Ungodly.”

Father, I’m so used to earning everything that grace is hard to believe. Thank You that You justify the ungodly, and that includes me. Help me rest in Your acceptance, and work hard because I’m loved, not to be loved. When I fail, remind me that my foundation is Jesus, not my results. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 21 — Count the Cost
fields.body_html:
“And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple. Which of you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?”

— Luke 14:27–28 (BSB)

Picture the scene. Jesus is popular. Large crowds are walking with Him down the road. Any normal leader would be thrilled and keep the mood high. Jesus turns around and says something that thins the crowd out.

He talks about a cross. In the first century nobody heard that word as jewellery or a nice symbol. A cross meant one thing: a man walking to his own execution. Jesus is saying that following Him is not a hobby you add to your week. It is a whole life handed over.

Then He tells a story about a tower. Most of us have seen one of these: a building that started with big plans and then stopped. Concrete pillars with steel rods sticking out of the top, rusting for years because the money ran out. Everyone who walks past knows the story. Somebody didn’t count the cost.

Jesus doesn’t want followers like that. He would rather you knew the price at the start than quit halfway.

So what can following Jesus cost a teenager? It might cost you the joke everyone else laughs at. It might cost you the group chat where people tear someone apart. It might cost you a weekend plan, a relationship that was pulling you away from God, or the easy popularity that comes from going along with everything. For some readers it costs far more. In some families and countries, choosing Jesus can mean anger at home, losing friends or real danger. If that’s you, Jesus is not surprised, and He has not left you alone.

Here’s why it’s not a trick. First, Jesus counted the cost before He asked you to. The Bible says that “for the joy set before Him” He “endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2). He never asks you to walk anywhere He hasn’t walked first.

Second, what you gain is bigger than what you give. Jesus told a story about a man who found treasure hidden in a field, and “in his joy he went and sold all he had and bought that field” (Matthew 13:44). Notice the word joy. The man wasn’t gritting his teeth. He had worked out the maths. fields.title: Day 22 — Standing Alone
fields.body_html:
“But Peter and John replied, ‘Judge for yourselves whether it is right in God’s sight to listen to you rather than God. For we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard.’”

— Acts 4:19–20 (BSB)

Peter and John had just been arrested. A man who had been unable to walk for over forty years was now on his feet, and the whole city was talking about it. The most powerful religious council in Jerusalem called them in and gave them a simple order: Stop talking about Jesus.

These were not trained speakers. The council noticed they were “unschooled, ordinary men” (Acts 4:13). They had no lawyers and no followers to protect them. A few weeks earlier, Peter had been so afraid that he swore he didn’t even know Jesus. Now he looks the council in the eye and says, in effect: You decide what’s right. We can’t stop.

What changed? The same verse tells us. The council “took note that these men had been with Jesus.” Courage didn’t come from their personalities. It came from Someone they had seen risen from the dead.

You probably won’t be dragged before a council. But you will face smaller versions of the same moment. A teacher mocks people who believe in God, and the class laughs. Your friends are planning something you know is wrong, and they’re waiting to see if you’re in. Someone posts a cruel video of a classmate and the whole group reacts with laughing faces, and yours is the only silence. It doesn’t feel like a big moment. It feels like being the only one.

Standing alone doesn’t mean being harsh or superior. Peter and John didn’t insult the council. They answered calmly and honestly. You can say no politely. You can say, “I’m not comfortable with that,” and leave it there. The point is not to win the argument. The point is to stay loyal to Jesus.

Christians have done this for two thousand years. Around the year 155, an old man named Polycarp was arrested for his faith in Smyrna, in what is now Turkey. The governor told him to curse Christ and go free. He replied, “Eighty and six years have I served him, and he never once wronged me; how then shall I blaspheme my King, Who hath saved me?” Christians in Africa, Asia, the Middle East and Latin America are still making that choice today, often at much greater cost than an awkward silence in a classroom.

Here’s the encouraging part. When you stand for Jesus, you are never actually alone. He promised, “surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). And often, you’ll find that someone else in the room was hoping a person would go first.

Courage is not the absence of fear. It’s what you do with your fear when you’ve been with Jesus.

Think about it: Where in your life right now is it hardest to be openly Christian? What would loyalty to Jesus look like there, without being harsh?

Try this: Decide now, before the moment comes, one sentence you’ll say when you’re pressured to do something wrong. Write it down and practise it.

Go deeper: Fox’s Book of Martyrs by John Foxe — the stories of the first Christians who would not deny Christ under Rome, including old Polycarp and a fifteen-year-old named Ponticus who stood firm alongside Blandina at Lyons. Start with chapter 2, “The Ten Primitive Persecutions.”

Lord Jesus, I want to be someone who has been with You. When I’m the only one, give me courage that is calm and kind, not proud. Help me remember Peter and John, Polycarp, and the brothers and sisters standing firm today. Thank You that You never leave me on my own. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 23 — Temptation
fields.body_html:
“When tempted, no one should say, ‘God is tempting me.’ For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone. But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.”

— James 1:13–15 (BSB)

Fishermen don’t throw a bare hook into the water. They hide it inside something the fish already wants. That’s the picture James uses. The word enticed is a fishing word: lured by bait.

Notice where James says the pull comes from. Not from God. Not mainly from the devil, though he is real. “Each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away.” The hook only works because something inside us wants the bait. That’s uncomfortable to admit, but it’s also freeing. It means temptation isn’t something that just happens to you, like weather. You can learn how it works in you.

James describes it like a life cycle. First there’s desire: a want, a craving, an itch. Then desire “conceives” — you stop just noticing it and start entertaining it, replaying it, planning it. Then it “gives birth to sin” — the action. And sin, left to grow up, “gives birth to death”: broken trust, a hard heart, distance from God.

So when do you fight? As early as possible. It’s much easier to drop a thought than to stop a plan. Think about a student who cheats in an exam. It rarely starts in the exam room. It starts weeks earlier with the thought everyone else does it, then a saved photo of the answers “just in case.” By exam day the battle was already lost.

Here are some honest strategies.

Name it. Say to yourself, or to God, “This is temptation.” Bait loses some of its power when you see the hook.

Change your location. When Joseph was tempted, “he escaped and ran outside” (Genesis 39:12). Sometimes the wisest thing is to physically leave — the room, the app, the conversation.

Answer with truth. When Jesus was tempted in the desert, He answered each time with Scripture: “Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4). Truth you know by heart is a weapon you always have.

Bring it into the light. Temptation loves secrecy. Telling a trusted Christian friend or adult breaks its grip.

And remember: being tempted is not the same as sinning. Jesus Himself was “tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). Feeling the pull doesn’t make you a failure. It makes you human. And if you do fall, the door back is wide open: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

One more thing. You don’t fight alone. “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7) comes right after “Submit yourselves, then, to God.” Strength to resist comes from being close to Him.

Think about it: What “bait” works best on you? At what stage — desire, entertaining it, or action — do you usually notice what’s happening?

Try this: Pick one temptation you face often and write down your plan: what you’ll do the moment you notice it, and one verse you’ll say.

Go deeper: The Mortification of Sin in Believers by John Owen — a seventeenth-century classic arguing that even the strongest Christians must fight sin every day, by the Spirit’s power: “be killing sin or it will be killing you.” It’s demanding reading; start with chapter 3, “The necessity of mortification: the duty of the best believers.”

Father, thank You that You never tempt me, and that Jesus understands every pull I feel. Help me see the hook inside the bait, and to run when I need to run. When I fall, help me come straight back to You instead of hiding. Make me strong by staying close to You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 24 — Purity
fields.body_html:
“For it is God’s will that you should be holy: You must abstain from sexual immorality; each of you must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor… For God has not called us to impurity, but to holiness.”

— 1 Thessalonians 4:3–4, 7 (BSB)

People often ask, “What is God’s will for my life?” and imagine it’s a mystery only revealed after years of prayer. Paul says, Here’s one part of it, plainly: “it is God’s will that you should be holy.”

Being pure isn’t about being naïve, or pretending you don’t have feelings. As you grow up, new and strong desires arrive. That’s not shameful. God designed your body and your sexuality, and He called His creation “very good.” Desire isn’t the enemy. But like fire, it’s good in the right place and destructive in the wrong one. God’s design is for sex to belong within marriage between a husband and wife, and He asks us to honour that with our bodies, our eyes and our minds — now, not just later.

Paul says each of us “must know how to control his own body in holiness and honor.” Know how suggests something learned. Nobody is born with self-control. It’s practised, the way you practise an instrument or a sport.

Let’s be honest about the world you live in. Sexual content is everywhere, and much of it can reach a phone in seconds. Pornography is one of the biggest battles for teenagers everywhere, and it trains the mind to see people as objects rather than as people made in God’s image. If that’s already a struggle for you, you are not a freak, and you are not beyond help. Shame tells you to hide. Jesus tells you to come into the light.

Some practical wisdom:

Decide ahead of time. The middle of a moment is the worst place to make a decision. Choose your boundaries now — with your phone, with what you watch, with how far is too far in a relationship.

Use the guardrails. Keep your phone out of your bedroom at night. Talk with a parent about filters and settings. This isn’t about being weak. Smart people put barriers where they know they’re vulnerable.

Guard your heart, not just your actions. “Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

Talk to someone. A parent, or a trusted adult at church, has heard it all before. Questions about your body, relationships or something you saw belong with them, not with the internet.

And hear this clearly: if anyone pressures you, sends you things you don’t want, asks you for pictures, or touches you in a way that’s wrong, it is not your fault. Tell a trusted adult right away, even if you’ve been told to keep it secret.

If you’ve already gone further than you wish you had, purity is not lost forever. David, after his worst failure, prayed, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10). God still answers that prayer. Purity is not a scoreboard. It’s a direction you walk, with Him.

Think about it: Where are you most vulnerable — a time of day, a place, an app? What guardrail would help?

Try this: Make one practical change today, such as charging your phone outside your bedroom tonight. If there’s something you need to talk about, choose the adult you’ll talk to this week.

Go deeper: Purity of Heart by William Booth — the founder of the Salvation Army reminds us that purity is bigger than one area of life: being “right and honest and true inside and out,” a heart with nothing else mixed in. Start with chapter 1, “Purity: What It Is.”

Holy God, thank You for making me, body and mind, and calling it good. I want to be holy because You are holy. Give me self-control, wisdom with my phone and my eyes, and courage to bring my struggles into the light. Where I have failed, wash me and create in me a clean heart. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 25 — What You Post
fields.body_html:
“Act wisely toward outsiders, redeeming the time. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone.”

— Colossians 4:5–6 (BSB)

Paul wrote these words long before anyone had a phone, but they fit a comment section perfectly.

Think about how much of your speech now happens with your thumbs. Messages, comments, captions, reactions, status updates, voice notes. Words you’d never say to someone’s face become strangely easy to type. A screenshot can travel across your whole school in an hour and stay online for years. And Jesus once warned that “men will give an account on the day of judgment for every careless word they have spoken” (Matthew 12:36). That includes typed ones.

Paul gives three tests.

Is it gracious? Gracious speech gives people more kindness than they’ve earned. It doesn’t pile on when someone is already being mocked. It doesn’t add the clever, cutting reply that gets the most laughs. Before you post, try asking: Would I say this if the person was standing next to me? Would I say it if Jesus was reading over my shoulder? (He is.)

Is it seasoned with salt? Salt makes food taste better, and in the ancient world it also kept food from going bad. Seasoned words aren’t bland or fake. They have flavour, honesty, even humour. But they preserve rather than rot. Gossip rots. Rumours rot. A pile-on rots. Words that make people feel seen, encouraged or pointed toward what’s true are salty in the best way.

Is it wise toward outsiders? People who don’t follow Jesus are watching how His followers talk. If your profile says you’re a Christian and your comments are full of contempt, the message they receive is not the gospel. On the other hand, a Christian who is consistently kind online, who refuses to join cruelty and isn’t afraid to say something good about Jesus, makes people curious.

There’s also the phrase “redeeming the time.” Paul means making the most of every opportunity. Scrolling can eat hours without you noticing. Some of that time could be redeemed: a message to a friend who’s struggling, a word of thanks, an encouragement to someone who never gets one.

A few habits that help:

  • Wait before you hit send when you’re angry. A message written in anger usually reads worse in the morning.
  • Don’t screenshot to shame. Private words shared to embarrass someone are a betrayal, even if the original was bad.
  • Leave group chats that are built around mocking people, or be the one who says, “That’s not fair.”
  • Ask what your profile preaches. Not with Bible verses, but with the tone of everything you share.

“When words are many, sin is unavoidable, but he who restrains his lips is wise” (Proverbs 10:19). Sometimes the most Christlike post is the one you don’t make.

Think about it: If someone who didn’t know you read your last fifty messages and comments, what would they guess about Jesus?

Try this: Today, use your phone to bless someone on purpose: send one specific, honest encouragement to a person who probably doesn’t expect it.

Go deeper: The Imitation of Christ by Thomas à Kempis — written six centuries before social media, it asks why we chatter so much “when we so seldom part without a troubled conscience,” and urges us to speak only when we have something that will build others up. Start with chapter 11, “Avoiding Idle Talk.”

Lord Jesus, You never spoke a careless word. Make my words gracious and seasoned with salt, online and offline. Stop me before I post something cruel, and help me use my phone to encourage people instead. Let the way I talk make others curious about You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

Would I say it if Jesus was reading over my shoulder? (He is.) Is it seasoned with salt? Salt makes food taste better, and in the ancient world it also kept food from going bad. Seasoned words aren’t bland or fake. They have flavour, honesty, even humour. But they preserve rather than rot. Gossip rots. Rumours rot. A pile-on rots. Words that make people feel seen, encouraged or pointed toward what’s true are salty in the best way. Is it wise toward outsiders? People who don’t follow Jesus are watching how His followers talk. If your profile says you’re a Christian and your comments are full of contempt, the message they receive is not the gospel. On the other hand, a Christian who is consistently kind online, who refuses to join cruelty and isn’t afraid to say something good about Jesus, makes people curious. There’s also the phrase “redeeming the time.” Paul means making the most of every opportunity. Scrolling can eat hours without you noticing. Some of that time could be redeemed: a message to a friend who’s struggling, a word of thanks, an encouragement to someone who never gets one. Private words shared to embarrass someone are a betrayal, even if the original was bad. Leave group chats that are built around mocking people, or be the one who says, “That’s not fair.” Ask what your profile preaches. Stop me before I post something cruel, and help me use my phone to encourage people instead. Let the way I talk make others curious about You. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 26 — Friends Who Shape You
fields.body_html:
“A righteous man is cautious in friendship, but the ways of the wicked lead them astray.”

— Proverbs 12:26 (BSB)

You become like the people you spend time with. You probably know this already. You pick up your friends’ phrases, their humour, the music they like, the way they talk about teachers and parents. It happens without anyone deciding it. That’s exactly why it matters.

Proverbs says it bluntly in another place: “He who walks with the wise will become wise, but the companion of fools will be destroyed” (Proverbs 13:20). And today’s verse says a righteous person is “cautious in friendship.” Not suspicious of everyone. Not cold. Cautious, meaning thoughtful about who gets close.

Here’s a helpful way to think about it. Jesus was friendly with everyone. He ate with tax collectors and outcasts. People who were rejected by everyone else felt welcome with Him. But He had an inner circle of twelve, and within that, three closest friends. You can be kind to everyone in your class, your team and your neighbourhood. That’s what Jesus did. But the people you let shape your heart should be chosen with care.

How do you tell a friend who makes you better from one who’s slowly pulling you away from God? A few questions:

  • After time with them, are you closer to God or further away?
  • Do they respect your faith, or mock it? A true friend won’t make you feel ashamed of following Jesus.
  • Can they hear “no” from you without punishing you for it?
  • Do they tell you the truth, even when it stings? “The wounds of a friend are faithful” (Proverbs 27:6).
  • Are they the same person when you’re not around? Someone who gossips to you will gossip about you.

Some of these questions might be uncomfortable. Maybe you’ve realised a friendship is dragging you somewhere you don’t want to go. That doesn’t mean you have to announce a dramatic break-up or treat them badly. Sometimes it means spending a bit less time together, changing where you hang out, or being honest about what you won’t do. Keep praying for them. Keep being kind. Just stop letting them steer.

Maybe the hard part for you is the opposite: you don’t have many friends at all, and the idea of being “cautious” sounds like a luxury. If that’s you, ask God for one good friend. It’s a prayer He loves to answer. Look around your church or youth group for someone else who seems a bit on the edge. Very often the friend you need is waiting for someone else to go first.

And remember what Proverbs says about the best Friend: “there is a friend who stays closer than a brother” (Proverbs 18:24). Jesus called His disciples “friends” (John 15:15). Whoever else comes and goes, He is the friend who stays.

Then aim to be the kind of friend you’re hoping to find.

Think about it: Which of your friends makes it easier to follow Jesus? Which makes it harder? What kind of friend are you to them?

Try this: Message one friend who makes you better and tell them so, specifically. If you need a friend like that, pray by name for one person you could get to know.

Go deeper: Growing in Wisdom — a practical guide for students on choosing friends, recognising toxic friendships and saying no to peer pressure, with real stories from Uganda, including a girl who refused to buy leaked exam papers when her classmates mocked her. Start with chapter 8, “Friendship and Peer Pressure.”

Lord Jesus, thank You for calling me Your friend. Help me be kind to everyone but wise about who shapes my heart. Give me friends who draw me closer to You, and give me the courage to change friendships that are pulling me away. Make me that kind of friend to someone else. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 27 — Parents
fields.body_html:
“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. ‘Honor your father and mother’ (which is the first commandment with a promise), ‘that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth.’”

— Ephesians 6:1–3 (BSB)

Let’s be honest: this might be the day you were tempted to skip.

The teenage years are when many people clash with their parents the most. You’re growing up, forming your own views and wanting more freedom. Your parents are trying to protect you, sometimes too tightly, sometimes awkwardly, sometimes while dealing with stress you don’t see. Doors get slammed. Phones get confiscated. Both sides say things they regret.

Into that tension, Paul writes two words: obey and honour.

They aren’t quite the same. Obedience is about actions: doing what your parents ask. Honour is about attitude: treating them with respect, recognising their God-given place in your life. As you get older, the details of obedience change. An adult son or daughter doesn’t need permission to go out. But honour never expires.

Notice the phrase “in the Lord.” Paul is not saying parents are perfect, or that they replace God. He’s saying: obey them as part of following Jesus. It’s an act of worship. The rare exception is if a parent tells you to do something clearly wrong. God’s authority is higher, and you should talk to another trusted adult.

Jesus Himself lived this. At twelve years old He had a misunderstanding with His parents in the temple. He was right and they were confused. Yet afterwards “He went down to Nazareth with them and was obedient to them” (Luke 2:51). The Son of God honoured an ordinary carpenter and his young wife.

What does honour look like for you?

  • Tone. You can disagree without contempt. Eye-rolling, sarcasm and silent treatment dishonour, even if you technically obey.
  • Speaking well of them when they’re not there, instead of joining friends who mock their parents.
  • Asking, not demanding. “Can we talk about my curfew?” goes further than a fight.
  • Noticing what they give. Many parents work long hours, give up things for you, or carry worries they’d never tell you.

It’s worth saying clearly: every family looks different. Maybe you live with one parent, grandparents, an aunt or uncle, a foster family or older siblings. Maybe a parent has left, or died, or is far away working. God’s command to honour applies to the people He has put in your life to care for you, and He is “a father of the fatherless” (Psalm 68:5) for every gap.

And this matters: if anyone at home hurts you, threatens you or makes you feel unsafe, that is not honour, and it is not your fault. Tell a trusted adult, such as a teacher, a pastor or a relative, right away. Honouring parents never means keeping that kind of secret.

Paul also wrote to parents in the next verse: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath” (Ephesians 6:4). God sees both sides. Your part is the one you can control.

Think about it: What does your tone usually say to your parents or guardians? Is there something you need to apologise for?

Try this: Do one thing today that shows honour without being asked: a job done, a thank-you said, or an apology given.

Go deeper: Susanna Wesley by Eliza Clarke — the story of the mother of nineteen children, including John and Charles Wesley, who made time every week to talk alone with each child about their life and faith. Start with chapter 9, “The Home Rebuilt.”

Father in heaven, thank You for the people You’ve given to care for me. Help me honour them with my words and my tone, even when we disagree. Forgive me for the times I’ve been disrespectful. Where my family is broken, be my Father, and give me wisdom and courage to speak up if I’m ever unsafe. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 28 — Prayer When It’s Boring
fields.body_html:
“But when you pray, go into your inner room, shut your door, and pray to your Father, who is unseen. And your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans, for they think that by their many words they will be heard. Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.”

— Matthew 6:6–8 (BSB)

Can we admit something? Sometimes prayer is boring.

You close your eyes, start to pray, and within a minute you’re thinking about the match, the test, the message you haven’t answered. You say the same words you said yesterday. It feels like talking to the ceiling. And because prayer is supposed to be important, you feel guilty about finding it dull, which makes you avoid it, which makes it feel even more distant.

If that’s you, you’re in very good company. Even Jesus’ closest friends asked, “Lord, teach us to pray” (Luke 11:1). Prayer is something you learn.

Look at what Jesus teaches here.

Prayer is to a Father. Three times in these verses Jesus says Father. You aren’t filling in a form or performing for an audience. You’re talking with Someone who loves you and already “knows what you need before you ask Him.” That takes the pressure off. You don’t need impressive words. You just need to show up.

Prayer needs a place. “Go into your inner room, shut your door.” Not everyone has a room of their own. Many readers share a room with brothers and sisters, or live in a busy home where there’s never quiet. Jesus Himself often had no private room, so He “frequently withdrew to the wilderness to pray” (Luke 5:16). Your inner room might be a walk to school, a bench at the edge of the field, the roof, or the few minutes before everyone else wakes up. The point is a door shut on distractions — and for most of us that means the phone face down or in another room.

Prayer isn’t about many words. Jesus says not to “babble on.” Long prayers aren’t more powerful. Some days the best prayer is short and honest: “God, I’m tired. I don’t feel much. But I’m here.”

Here are some ways to fight the boredom:

  • Pray out loud, quietly, or walk while you pray. It keeps your mind from wandering.
  • Write your prayers down. A notebook gives your thoughts somewhere to land, and later you’ll see answers you would have forgotten.
  • Pray Scripture. Take a psalm and turn it into your own words. The invitation to “pour out your hearts before Him” (Psalm 62:8) means you can be completely honest.
  • Use a simple pattern: thank Him for something, tell Him something you’re sorry for, ask Him for something, and pray for someone else.
  • Keep a list of people and situations, and watch what God does.

And remember: when you don’t know what to say, “the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Even your weak prayers are carried.

Prayer isn’t always exciting. Neither is any deep relationship, every single day. But quiet faithfulness builds something strong underneath.

Think about it: Where and when could your “inner room” be? What usually distracts you most when you try to pray?

Try this: Tonight or tomorrow morning, put your phone in another room and pray for five minutes using the pattern: thanks, sorry, asking, others.

Go deeper: With Christ in the School of Prayer by Andrew Murray — Murray calls the inner room “Jesus’ schoolroom” and says the first thing to learn there is that you are meeting your Father. Start with chapter 4, “Alone with God.”

Father, sometimes I find prayer boring, and I’m sorry for how often I’d rather scroll than talk to You. Thank You that You already know what I need, and that You want to hear from me anyway. Teach me to pray. Help me find my inner room and keep showing up, even on the dull days. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 29 — Hearing God
fields.body_html:
“I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go; I will give you counsel and watch over you.”

— Psalm 32:8 (BSB)

What subjects should I choose? Should I take this job? Should I go out with this person? Where should I study, or should I study at all? Should I move to the city with my cousin?

Big decisions start arriving in your teenage years, and they can feel terrifying. Many Christians wish God would just send a text: Do this. Instead, it can seem like He’s silent, and you’re left guessing.

But look at this promise. “I will instruct you and teach you the way you should go.” God isn’t hiding His will to test you. He wants to guide you more than you want to be guided. The verse goes on: “I will give you counsel and watch over you.” The picture is a teacher or coach who keeps an eye on you as you walk.

So how does God guide? Usually not by a voice from the sky, though He is free to speak however He likes. Most often He uses several things together.

His Word. This is the clearest way God speaks. “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path” (Psalm 119:105). God will never lead you to do something His Word calls wrong. If you’re asking “Should I lie about this?” you already have your answer. Many of your big questions are settled by things the Bible makes plain: honesty, kindness, purity, serving others.

Prayer and the Spirit’s quiet nudges. Jesus said, “My sheep listen to My voice; I know them, and they follow Me” (John 10:27). As you pray and read, you may sense a growing peace about one direction, or a lack of peace about another. Be careful here. Feelings can be mistaken, so test them against Scripture.

Wise people. Parents, pastors, teachers and mature Christian friends can see what you can’t. Ask them.

Circumstances. God opens and closes doors. Paul once tried to go somewhere, and “the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them” (Acts 16:7). A door that slams shut can be God’s guidance too.

A pastor called F. B. Meyer said that when God’s Word, the inner prompting of His Spirit and our circumstances line up, we can move forward with confidence. And when they don’t yet agree? His advice was simple: “If you do not know what you ought to do, stand still until you do.”

Two more things. First, God is more interested in who you are becoming than in which school you choose. Often there are several good options, and any of them can honour Him. Second, the starting point is surrender. It’s hard to hear God’s direction when you’ve already decided. Pray honestly, “Lord, I want what You want,” and mean it. “Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

Think about it: What decision is on your mind right now? Have you honestly asked God, and what has His Word already made clear about it?

Try this: Write down a decision you’re facing. Under it, write what Scripture says, what wise people have told you, what circumstances suggest, and what you sense in prayer. Then ask someone you trust to look at it with you.

Go deeper: The Secret of Guidance by F. B. Meyer — a short, wise guide to knowing God’s will: pure motives, a surrendered will, prayer, and waiting until God’s Word, His Spirit and your circumstances agree. Start with chapter 1, “The Secret of Guidance.”

Father, thank You for promising to teach me the way I should go. I bring You my decisions, big and small. Make Your Word clear to me, give me wise people to listen to, and help me trust You when the way isn’t clear yet. I want what You want. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Day 30 — Anchored
fields.body_html:
“Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess, for He who promised is faithful.”

— Hebrews 10:23 (BSB)

Thirty days ago, this book started with a question: Is it true? You’ve looked at doubt, evidence, suffering and science. You’ve asked Who am I? and heard what God says about your worth, your failures and where you belong. And over these last ten days, you’ve seen what following Jesus for real looks like: counting the cost, standing alone, fighting temptation, guarding your words and your heart, honouring your family, praying and listening.

Now, one last picture. It’s the picture this whole book is named after.

The writer of Hebrews says: “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure” (Hebrews 6:19). Anyone who has lived near the sea, or a big lake, knows what an anchor does. It doesn’t stop the storm. The wind still blows and the waves still rise. But a boat that’s anchored doesn’t get swept onto the rocks. It holds.

Notice what holds you. It’s not how strong your faith feels today. It’s not your track record or your mood. An anchor works because it grips something solid outside the boat. Hebrews says this hope “enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf.” In other words, your anchor is fastened to Jesus Himself, in the very presence of God. The rope runs from your life to Him.

That’s why today’s verse can say, “Let us hold resolutely to the hope we profess.” And look at the reason: “for He who promised is faithful.” You hold on because He is faithful. Even on the days your grip feels weak, He does not let go. Jesus said, “the one who comes to Me I will never drive away” (John 6:37).

Storms are coming. That’s not pessimism. It’s honesty. Jesus Himself said, “In the world you will have tribulation.” But He didn’t stop there: “But take courage; I have overcome the world!” (John 16:33). There will be exams that go badly, friendships that break, family troubles, doubts that come back at night, and losses you can’t imagine yet. Being anchored doesn’t mean none of that touches you. It means none of it can carry you away.

So how do you keep an anchored life? The same way you’ve practised this month. Keep reading His Word. Keep praying, even on boring days. Keep close to other believers. Keep confessing quickly when you fall. Keep asking your hard questions out loud, to Him and to wise people. None of these is the anchor. But they keep you aware of the One who is.

And if you finish this book still unsure — that’s all right. Keep holding on. Keep asking. “He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion” (Philippians 1:6). He is not finished with you.

You are anchored. Not because you’re strong, but because He is faithful.

Think about it: Looking back over these thirty days, what is one truth that has anchored you most? Which day would you want to read again?

Try this: Write Hebrews 6:19 somewhere you’ll see it every day: a lock screen, a mirror or the inside of a notebook. Then tell one person what this month has meant to you.

Go deeper: Absolute Surrender by Andrew Murray — Murray shows that God keeps not only an inheritance in heaven for us, but keeps us for it, every moment, through faith. Start with chapter 8, “Kept by the Power of God.”

Faithful God, thank You for these thirty days. Thank You that my hope is anchored in Jesus, firm and secure, and that You hold on to me even when my grip is weak. When storms come, keep me steady. Help me keep reading, praying and following You for real, all my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion: Holding Fast
fields.body_html:
You made it. Thirty days. Whether you read one a day without missing, or took three months and skipped a few, you’ve done something many people never do: you’ve sat down, opened God’s Word and asked honest questions.

Think back over the road you’ve walked.

In Part 1, you asked Is it true? You learned that doubt is allowed, and that Christianity isn’t afraid of hard questions. You looked at the reasons to believe in God, the reliability of the Bible, the historical Jesus and the evidence for His resurrection. You faced the hardest question of all, suffering, and found a God who doesn’t stand far away from pain but entered it Himself.

In Part 2, you asked Who am I? You heard that you are made in God’s image, known completely and loved anyway. That your worth isn’t measured by your feed, your grades or how you compare to others. That when you’ve blown it, Jesus comes looking for you, the way He came for Peter on the beach. That you belong to a family, and that God has adopted you as His own child.

In Part 3, you looked at what it means to follow Jesus for real: in your temptations, your purity, your posts, your friendships, your family, your prayers and your decisions.

Through all of it, one thing has stayed the same. It was never really about how strong you are. It’s about how faithful He is.

If you haven’t trusted Jesus yet

Maybe you’ve read this whole book from the outside, curious, unsure or still deciding. Thank you for reading honestly. Here’s the heart of it, as simply as we can say it.

God made you and loves you. All of us have turned away from Him, and that sin separates us from Him. But “God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Jesus died in your place and rose again. Forgiveness and new life aren’t something you earn. They are a gift you receive. The Bible promises that “to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12).

If you want to trust Jesus, you can tell Him so, right now, in your own words. You might pray something like this: Jesus, I believe You died for me and rose again. I’m sorry for my sin. I want to follow You. Please forgive me and make me Yours. If you pray that and mean it, tell a Christian you trust — a parent, a pastor, a youth leader or a friend. You’re not meant to walk this road alone.

Keep going

Don’t let this be the end of your time with God each day. Keep reading the Bible. A good place to start is the Gospel of Mark, a short chapter a day, or a psalm each morning. Keep praying, even when it’s boring. Keep showing up at church or youth group.

And try one of the classics from the Go deeper sections. These books have helped Christians for hundreds of years. The Pilgrim’s Progress (For Teens) is a great place to start. With Christ in the School of Prayer will change how you pray. Pick one, and read a chapter a week.

Coming next: Book 2

Anchored Book 1 was about the foundations: is it true, who am I, and what does it look like to follow Jesus. Book 2, “Real Life,” takes those foundations into the messy places: anxiety, screens, dating, family conflict, grief, failure and anger. They’re the things that test an anchor, and the God who held you here will hold you there too.

Until then, hold fast. He who promised is faithful.

Lord Jesus, thank You for walking with me through these thirty days. Thank You for answering my questions, telling me who I am and showing me how to follow You. Anchor my soul in You, firm and secure, whatever storms are coming. Keep me reading Your Word, keep me praying and keep me close to You for the rest of my life. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
